title: Skyr: protein, calories and nutrition

seo.title: Skyr nutrition: protein, calories and sugar
seo.meta_description: A current plain skyr provides 17 g protein and 120 calories per 150 g. See how skyr concentrates protein and how whole-milk and flavored versions differ.
seo.search_intent: Understand skyr protein, calories and nutrition

excerpt: Plain skyr can pack a large amount of protein into a small cup. Icelandic Provisions Plain Skyr currently provides 17 g protein, 120 calories, 2.5 g fat and 3 g sugar per 150 g—about 11.3 g protein and 80 calories per 100 g.
content_html:
Skyr looks like thick yogurt, but its most useful nutrition feature is concentration: a relatively small serving can provide a lot of milk protein.

A current plain skyr label

Icelandic Provisions Plain Skyr lists per 150 g cup:

  • 120 calories
  • 17 g protein
  • 2.5 g fat
  • 3 g total sugar
  • 0 g added sugar
  • 190 mg calcium

Normalized to 100 g, that is about 80 calories and 11.3 g protein.

Why is protein so high?

Traditional skyr production ferments milk and removes whey, concentrating milk solids. Modern commercial processes vary, but the dense protein profile remains a defining practical feature.

The name is not enough: plain, flavored and fat level

The same brand's vanilla skyr provides 15 g protein and 130 calories per 150 g, with 6 g added sugar. Flavoring does not make skyr nutritionally bad, but it changes what the cup contains.

Whole Milk Plain Skyr from the same company has 6 g fat and 130 calories per 170 g. The word “skyr” does not guarantee one fat level.

How to read a skyr label without assuming every cup is the same

Skyr's reputation for protein comes from concentrating milk solids and using a cultured process that produces a thick product. Plain versions can deliver a substantial amount of protein in a modest calorie range, especially when made from low-fat milk. But the category includes full-fat, flavored, fruit-on-the-bottom, and dessert-like versions too. A vanilla or berry skyr may still be protein-rich while carrying noticeably more added sugar than the plain tub beside it.

Serving size matters because packages are not standardized. One brand may sell a 150 g cup, another a 170 g cup, and a large tub may list nutrition per 100 g. Comparing protein per 100 g is useful when you want to judge concentration; comparing the amount you actually eat is more useful for meal planning. The same logic applies to calories, sugar, sodium, and calcium. “High protein” can be true while the absolute contribution changes substantially with portion size.

Calcium content can vary more than people expect after straining because minerals distribute between curd and whey and manufacturers may use different milk formulations. If calcium is important, read the label rather than assuming skyr automatically beats milk or yogurt. The same applies to live cultures: cultured products are made with bacteria, but whether particular organisms remain alive at meaningful levels through the end of shelf life depends on the product and its labeling.

Skyr can be useful beyond breakfast. Plain versions can replace sour cream in dips, add protein to smoothies, or provide a creamy base for sauces without much added fat. For someone trying to gain weight or who needs more energy, pairing a very lean skyr with nuts, seeds, granola, or fruit may make more sense than choosing the leanest food possible. Nutrition works at the meal level, so the “best” skyr is the one that helps the whole meal fit your needs.

Protein quality is another reason skyr can work well in a meal. Dairy protein provides all essential amino acids and contains a substantial share of leucine, which is relevant to muscle protein synthesis. That does not mean every snack needs skyr or that more protein is always better. Total daily intake, distribution across meals, exercise, age, and energy intake all matter.

If you use skyr as a substitute for yogurt in cooking, remember that very low-fat versions can behave differently under heat. They may split or taste sharper in hot sauces. Tempering the product, using gentle heat, or adding it after cooking can preserve texture. A food's nutrition label is only part of its usefulness; cooking behavior determines whether you will actually keep it in your routine.

People comparing brands should also check sodium and added sugar rather than focusing only on protein. Two cups with similar protein can differ markedly once flavoring and processing choices are included.

What is a realistic protein contribution?

One 150 g plain cup gives 17 g protein. That is more informative than quoting protein per 100 g when the package itself is a common single serving.

Skyr's appeal is therefore straightforward: concentrated dairy protein, usually with relatively little added sugar when plain.

faq.question: How much protein is in skyr?
faq.answer: The plain product used here provides 17 g per 150 g cup, about 11.3 g/100 g.

faq.question: How many calories are in skyr?
faq.answer: 120 calories per 150 g in the plain low-fat example.

faq.question: Does plain skyr have added sugar?
faq.answer: The product cited has 0 g added sugar and 3 g total sugar.

faq.question: Is all skyr nonfat?
faq.answer: No. Whole-milk versions exist and contain more fat and calories.
